title: Rereading Changing Our Minds and a Different Way to Learn
author: Educating Hatbeasts
summary: Educating Hatbeasts, a home-educating parent of disabled children, rereads two books by Dr. Naomi Fisher that make the case for self-directed education and a non-medical view of neurodivergence. The author finds the books warm and readable but argues that they sell a kind of miracle, in which normal-but-different children are wrongly identified as disabled and then cured by a committed parent. The review challenges specific evidence, such as the summer-born diagnosis effect, the claim that late readers catch up, and the framing of a restless child as simply who he is. It also criticises the linear Safe to Learn pyramid and the chapters on anxiety and demand avoidance for implying that things work out if parents get everything right. The author concedes that flexibility is enough for some children but insists that some children are disabled, and that this cohort is poorly served.
points: The central complaint is that the books describe a narrow group of children with school-induced anxiety and then imply the same cure works for children with real disabilities.
The review shows how cited statistics can support something different from what the author claims, such as late reading requiring worry later rather than none at all.
The Danish redshirting study is offered as a simple policy fix for summer-born disadvantage that the books omit.
The Safe to Learn pyramid is criticised as linear and as placing responsibility on parents to get every step right.
The author accepts that some children need only more flexibility, which keeps the critique focused on overreach rather than on self-directed education as a whole.
quotes: Yet a miracle is being sold here. It’s the story of how normal-but-different children are identified disabled and traumatised by the school environment and how, if you have such a child, self-directed education delivered by a committed parent can provide a miraculous cure.
I should mention upfront that, for some kids, more flexibility in mainstream or a different way to learn is doubtless enough to achieve their true educational potential.

What she doesn’t do is cite a 2018 international study of ADHD diagnoses that found Danish kids don’t have the same ‘summer-born’ effect, which the authors speculate is down to the national practice of ‘redshirting’, i.e. holding kids who seem to be immature back a year until they catch up.
Instead of not worrying about reading at all, self-directed educators just need to worry later: if their child visibly struggles, or, alternatively, ages well into the tail of Jo Isaac’s graph.
Sidney will still want to run in the corridors, whatever type of school he’s at. It just means it’s no longer a problem for the school and therefore no one is going to punish him for it.

The difficulty is the linear nature of the pyramid through which, slowly, the child rises until, at Stage Three, they blossom into fully-fledged self-directed learner able to steer their own education and rapidly acquire new skills.

Perhaps unintentionally, some of these latter chapters create the impression that self-directed education will always work out just fine for neurodivergent kids - provided parents do everything right.
